Normal DNA degeneration is slow, which is extremely expensive to measure. Presumably it was cheap to turn off DNA repair and use the DNA as a chemical clock.

The goal of this research was to study mitochondrial replacement more than normal aging. Surprisingly little is known about the birth and death of mitochondria. Can they be made to die? Can the dead ones be replaced? Do the replacements come from an idle, unused pool of mitochondria? Is there a way to measure replacement rate to see if interventions have an effect? With this research they have proven a technique for looking for answers.

Normal DNA degeneration is slow

We're not talking about nuclear DNA. The point of the study was that mitochondrial DNA isn't well maintained and does degenerate within a fruit fly's lifespan, or so I thought. This lifespan is only 45 days which definitely is within a lab's experimental horizon. If it doesn't actually degenerate significantly within that lifespan, I don't see what relevance it can have toward a fruit fly's aging. Is the GM fruit fly being used to model human aging rather than study actual aging in fruit flies?

This is not a cure for aging. This addresses one of many problems associated with cells as they age. A treatment from this would reduce deterioration of the brain and muscles as we age, but would not stop or reverse aging, or solve problems that come with immortality. For that, other things would still need to be solved, including:

The shortening of telomere caps, strokes and heart disease, dental decay/erosion, insulin resistance, and erosion of cartilage in joints.

That said, this could lead to massive quality of life improvements if we can keep our minds and our muscles well into old age. Remember, when you are injured, you never fully heal. You just mitigate and collect damage. On a long enough timeline, all those injuries and scar tissues add up.
